source_span: 10yr US real yields rising +9.8bps to a post-2008 high of 2.87% but 10yr breakevens actually falling by -1.3bps... So at face value there is no concern about longer-term inflation... In addition measures of term premium have been range bound for around 18 months so the sell-off isn't really fiscal related.
source_chain: Real yields rose (+9.8bp to 2.87%, +97bp YTD) while breakevens fell/were flat (-1.3bp, only +9bp YTD) therefore the sell-off is not an inflation story (breakevens aren't pricing more inflation despite oil +75%) therefore, with term premium range-bound ~18 months, it isn't a fiscal/deficit story either, leaving Reid's own read that breakevens are too low and real yields too high. No explicit falsifiable invalidation is stated for this specific read.
pulse_chain: Real yields rose 9.8bp to a post-2008 high of 2.87% while breakevens fell 1.3bp, and real yields are up 97bp on the year against 9bp for breakevens with term premium range-bound ~18 months, therefore the move is a growth/real-rate repricing, not an inflation move and not a deficit story, therefore banks split on what happens next (BofA: buy bonds on policymaker panic; Goldman's Pasquariello: short bonds against equity length), with the falsifiable line set at Goldman's own two-standard-deviation speed rule for when equities start reacting, cut against by CTAs already near max short (99-100%, ~$390bn) who would be squeezed rather than validated by a cool print.
why: The theme reproduces Reid's real-yield-vs-breakeven arithmetic and his explicit 'not inflation, not fiscal' conclusion in the same direction with correct attribution and figures, and layers a second, separately and correctly sourced Goldman mechanism (the speed rule and CTA positioning, both accurately quoted from d43/d48) as the invalidation rather than inventing one or misattributing either bank's argument.
